The United States Constitution does not mention removal, but Congress has conferred jurisdiction to hear removed cases since the First Judiciary
Act of 1789. The current general removal statute, 28 U.S.C. § 1441, traces to the Judiciary Act of 1875 and amendments enacted in 1887. See Collins,
The Unhappy History of Federal Question Removal, 71 Iowa L.Rev. 717 (1986). Special removal statutes have been enacted for specific parties and
claims. E.g., 28 U.S.C. § 1442 (removal by federal officers); 28 U.S.C. § 1443 (removal of certain cases involving civil rights); 28 U.S.C. § 1453
(removal of certain interstate class actions). Congress also has barred the removal of certain kinds of claims. E.g., 28 U.S.C. § 1445 (actions against
railroads under the Federal Employers’ Liability Act).
The possibility of removal gives defendants a significant veto power over plaintiff’s forum choice. See Bassett & Perschbacher, The Roots of
Removal, 77 Brooklyn L.Rev. 1, 2 (2011). The procedure is justified on a number of grounds. From the perspective of litigant equality, removal insures
that defendants as well as plaintiffs “decide which cases federal courts hear.” Haiber, Removing the Bias Against Removal, 53 Cath.U.L.Rev. 609, 611
(2004). Moreover, in diversity actions, removal protects an out-of-state defendant from the threat of local bias. However, it is not uncommon for a
defendant to base a decision to remove on tactical reasons, which, as one commentary explains, may include such considerations as “jury verdicts, trial
rules and procedure, and the availability, caseload and personality of federal judges.” Reggio, Removal and Remand: A Guide to Navigating Between
the State and Federal Courts, 23 Miss.L.Rev. 97, 98 (2004). The strategic significance of removal is underscored by empirical studies of win-loss rates
in removed actions. Plaintiff’s win rate for a case filed in federal court under diversity jurisdiction is 71 percent, but drops to 34 percent for a case filed
in state court and removed under diversity jurisdiction. See Clermont & Eisenberg, Do Case Outcomes Really Reveal Anything About the Legal
System? Win Rates and Removal Jurisdiction, 83 Cornell L.Rev. 581, 581, 593 (1998); see also Clermont, Litigation Realities Redux, 84 Notre Dame
L.Rev. 1919, 1927 (2009).

Section 1441(a) authorizes removal “by the defendant or the defendants.” SHAMROCK OIL & GAS CORP. v. SHEETS, 313 U.S.
100, 105–08, 61 S.Ct. 868, 871–72, 85 L.Ed. 1214, 1217–19 (1941), presented the question whether a plaintiff could remove a state court
action to the federal courts because defendant had interposed a federal counterclaim. Justice Stone, writing for a unanimous Court,
answered no:
